newsitem.title: USA: U.S. futures exchanges blast CFTC regulation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. futures exchanges blast CFTC regulation.

text.p: The two major Chicago futures exchanges accused Commodity Futures Exchange Commission of "micro-managing" their business and encouraging customers to move to overseas futures markets with less stringent regulatory requirements.
"They are not an oversight body, they are the micro-management of our industry," John Sandner, chairman of Chicago Mercantile Exchange, told a House Agriculture subcommittee.

Members of the subcommittee, chaired by Rep. Thomas Ewing, R-Ill., expressed concern at the loss of business on U.S. futures market but said they wanted to balance the needs of professional traders with protection for the public.
The hearing Tuesday was the first of three days of testimony on Ewing's proposed bill to strip the CFTC of most of its regulatory powers.

Sandner and the heads of Chicago Board of Trade, New York Mercantile Exchange and Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange testified on the bill, which closely resembles pending legislation in the Senate. The exchanges have lobbied on behalf of the legislation, saying they need regulatory relief to compete with fast-growing futures exchanges overseas.
In testimony earlier Tuesday, CFTC commissioner Brooksley Born reminded the subcommittee about the dangers of market manipulation in copper, silver, cattle and other futures in recent years.

At the hearing, the four exchanges promised they would continue collecting data and information about large trader and speculative positions to share with the CFTC, even if they were not required to by law. That has emerged as a major point of contention for the CFTC, which claims it would be powerless to investigate suspected fraud under the proposed legislation.

The CFTC contends that if the so-called professional market is exempted from regulation -- comprising about 90 percent of all U.S. futures traded -- the market will be vulnerable to manipulation. Currently, the agency requires the exchanges to collect daily data about large positions in the market, segregate client funds and maintain an audit trail of trades, among other regulations.
"The top exchanges in the world will be on foreign shores unless we get some kind of regulatory relief," Sandner said.

The LIFFE in London now claims to be the second biggest futures exchange in the world, overtaking the Chicago Mercantile Exchange. Some U.S. customers and traders have moved their business to London because of less paperwork required by the exchange, and its ability to introduce new contracts swiftly, Sandner said.
Five years ago, NYMEX had about 50 percent of the copper futures market in the world but that has dwindled to less than 10 percent today, said Daniel Rappaport, chairman of NYMEX.
"Soon there is going to be nothing left to regulate because the market is going to go overseas," Rappaport said.
For example, CBOT and CME each have about 110 employees in their respective audit departments, while the LIFFE has just 35, said Tom Donovan, president of CBOT.
The unregulated over-the-counter market has also drained away futures trading from the United States, they said.

The two Chicago exchanges tried to allay the concern of the subcommittee over farmers and ranchers in the futures market by saying they did not plan to include agricultural futures markets in the so-called "professional market" that would be exempted from regulation.
"It's not our intention to transform our existing agricultural markets into professional markets," Donovan said.

Under last year's farm legislation that phases out the longstanding system of price supports, U.S. farmers and ranchers are being encouraged by the Agriculture Department to investigate futures and other risk management techniques.
"No one would be hurt by this (legislation)," Sandner said in response to questioning by Rep. Jerry Moran (R-KS). "These are customers with large accounts who want less regulation."

Rep. Ed Bryant (R-Tenn) said he would support "as little regulation as possible" of the futures industry, a view echoed by several other members of the subcommittee. ((--Julie Vorman, Washington commodities desk, 202-898-8467))
